answer.summary: Conrad’s You Don’t Know Jack experience suggests that a generalist should keep their breadth, but build real depth and a track record in a clear area of responsibility. His technical role rewarded shipping high-quality software—not extra opinions on design or marketing—and that focus helped him develop strong engineering skills.

sections.heading: Make breadth a complement to a clear specialty
sections.content: At Apple, Conrad felt he had become “six miles wide and a centimeter deep.” At Berkeley Systems, he could still weigh in on game design or marketing, but his job as technical director was to build the software on time and at high quality. Those broader contributions did not make up for failing at that core responsibility. For a generalist, the practical takeaway is to clarify what you are accountable for and make your broad perspective additive—not a substitute for delivering in that lane. This is a synthesis of Conrad’s experience.

sections.heading: Use focused work to build demonstrable depth
sections.content: Conrad described being forced to go deep as a blessing: he spent time developing as an engineering manager and wrote a lot of software, eventually feeling he could hold his own technically. He said his college education and the amount of software he wrote at Apple had not been enough to get him there. He also saw value in cultures with “swim lanes,” where people are encouraged to become exceptional in their lane. So, if you tend to generalize, seek work that lets you practice a core skill repeatedly and be judged on concrete results; keep contributing across functions, but don’t let that prevent you from building depth. This is a synthesis of his advice and experience, not a guarantee of career success.
